title: Semi-supervised Hopfield model: Theoretical and Numerical results
summary: In the daily practice of Machine Learning, fully labeled datasets are a luxury: labels demand expensive and time-consuming human annotation, whereas raw, unlabeled data can be harvested automatically and in bulk. Semi-supervised learning, where the network jointly exploits the few labeled and the many unlabeled examples at its disposal, is the standard answer to this asymmetry, yet a statistical mechanical theory of semi-supervised Hebbian learning is still lacking. In this paper we fill this gap for the Hopfield network: we prescribe a synaptic coupling given by the convex combination, weighted by a mixing parameter λin [0,1], of the supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels built from the same archetypes, and we solve for the emergent computational capabilities of the resulting network. A signal-to-noise analysis yields the one-step Mattis magnetization and the learning threshold, i.e. the minimum dataset size for stable retrieval. Using Guerra's interpolation, we then derive the Replica Symmetric quenched pressure in the high-storage regime, treating the correlated disorder generated by the supervised and unsupervised channels through a particular eigen-channel decomposition. The resulting phase diagram shows that a mixed strategy outperforms both pure protocols. Finally, we prove that the quenched pressure is convex in λ, so thermodynamics cannot select an interior mixture: λis therefore a learning hyperparameter. All the analytical findings are successfully checked against extensive Monte Carlo simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a statistical mechanical theory for semi-supervised Hebbian learning in Hopfield networks, where the synaptic coupling is a convex combination of supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels weighted by a mixing parameter λ. The authors derive the one-step Mattis magnetization, learning threshold, and Replica Symmetric quenched pressure in the high-storage regime, showing that a mixed strategy outperforms both pure protocols, and proving that the free energy is convex in λ (so λ acts as a hyperparameter rather than being thermodynamically selected).
AI.motivation: Fully labeled datasets are expensive and scarce while unlabeled data is abundant, motivating semi-supervised learning. However, a statistical mechanical theory of semi-supervised Hebbian learning is lacking. This paper fills this gap for the Hopfield network by analyzing a synaptic coupling that blends supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels.
AI.method: The authors prescribe a synaptic coupling as a convex combination (weighted by λ∈[0,1]) of supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels built from the same archetypes. They use signal-to-noise analysis for the one-step Mattis magnetization and learning threshold, and Guerra's interpolation to derive the Replica Symmetric quenched pressure in the high-storage regime. Correlated disorder from the two channels is handled via an eigen-channel decomposition.
AI.result: The phase diagram shows that a mixed strategy (blending supervised and unsupervised terms) outperforms both pure protocols. The quenched pressure is proved to be convex in λ, meaning thermodynamics cannot select an interior mixture—λ remains a learning hyperparameter. All analytical results are verified against extensive Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.conclusion: Semi-supervised Hebbian learning in Hopfield networks is theoretically tractable and advantageous: mixing supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels yields better performance than either alone. Since the quenched free energy is convex in λ, the optimal mixing is at the boundary, making λ a tunable hyperparameter rather than a thermodynamically self-selected quantity.

title: Geometry-Induced Domain-Wall Pinning and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Asymmetry in Nominally One-Dimensional Rydberg Arrays
summary: We perform experiments on QuEra's neutral-Rydberg-atom Aquila quantum computer, using quasi-adiabatic evolution on 1-dimensional models. We use hardware fine-tuning to balance the measurement statistics close to zero net magnetization, in two different geometric outlines: one closed triangular model with 33 atoms, and one 47-atom square with an engineered atom vacancy. The nature of this processor restricts the geometry of the atoms that can be programmed to a 2D plane. We report effects not predicted by the pure 1D Ising model, such as pinning of domain walls and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking due to the interplay between van der Waals interactions and the Rydberg blockade. In particular, atoms around the atom vacancy and at the vertices of the 1-dimensional square-outline model strongly prefer the Rydberg state, leading to the effective model having a ferromagnetic bond across the vacancy.

AI.tldr: Experiments on QuEra's Aquila neutral-Rydberg-atom quantum computer using quasi-adiabatic evolution on 1D models reveal effects not predicted by pure 1D Ising models, including domain wall pinning and Z2 symmetry breaking due to van der Waals interactions and Rydberg blockade, with atoms near vacancies and vertices preferring the Rydberg state.
AI.motivation: To probe the behavior of 1D quasi-adiabatic evolution on a real quantum processor and uncover physics beyond the idealized 1D Ising model, given the geometric constraints of the neutral-atom platform.
AI.method: Experiments on QuEra's Aquila quantum computer using quasi-adiabatic evolution on 1D models with hardware fine-tuning of measurement statistics near zero net magnetization. Two geometries: a 33-atom closed triangular model and a 47-atom square with an engineered atom vacancy.
AI.result: Observation of effects not predicted by the pure 1D Ising model, including domain wall pinning and Z2 symmetry breaking. Atoms around vacancies and at square vertices strongly prefer the Rydberg state, producing an effective ferromagnetic bond across the vacancy.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between van der Waals interactions and Rydberg blockade in the neutral-atom processor introduces geometric and interaction effects that go beyond the idealized 1D Ising description, highlighting material-specific physics in analog quantum simulation.

title: Designing tight frames for quantum computing
comment: Licenciatura thesis, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, 2024. Advisor: Dardo Goyeneche. 65 pages
summary: The aim of this thesis is to explore the implementation of a special kind of quantum measurements, so called harmonic tight frames. To achieve this goal, representation theory is addressed, emphasizing its construction from irreducible representations and the relations they satisfy. These tools simplify the study due to the existence of symmetries, leading to the concept of group frames, defined as orbits under the unitary action of a group and characterized by their symmetry groups. Among the various groups, the simplest are the abelian ones, giving rise to harmonic frames, which are analyzed through the classification theorem of abelian groups and the characters of their irreducible representations. In the quantum mechanics context, the frame elements can be interpreted as pure states of a system. Therefore, the necessary and sufficient conditions for separability are explored, as separable states are easier to implement due to their local nature. Alternatively, when viewing frames as measurements, the concept of POVMs and Naimark's theorem are studied as key tools for designing measurements in quantum computers. Using this knowledge, a characterization of the harmonic frames is given from the abelian group structure theorem, which allows obtaining a necessary and sufficient condition for their separability. The conditions of maximum entanglement of these states for bipartite systems are also studied, obtaining a necessary condition on the dimensions of the subsystems. Finally, a quantum circuit is obtained that allows implementing the harmonic frames associated to cyclic groups as POVMs using a Fourier matrix and a permutation matrix. We conclude by giving simple examples where the results are applied to quantum computers and proposing future avenues of research that could serve to improve the circuit design and extend it to the case of all harmonic frames.

AI.tldr: This thesis explores harmonic tight frames as quantum measurements, using representation theory and abelian group classification to characterize their separability and entanglement properties, and provides a quantum circuit implementation of harmonic frames associated to cyclic groups as POVMs using Fourier and permutation matrices.
AI.motivation: The goal is to understand and implement harmonic tight frames as quantum measurements, motivated by their relevance to quantum computing and quantum information, where frame elements represent pure states and frames serve as measurements (POVMs).
AI.method: The approach uses representation theory and irreducible representations to simplify frame analysis via symmetries, introduces group frames as unitary orbits, and analyzes harmonic frames (abelian group frames) through the classification theorem of abelian groups and character theory. Separability conditions are studied, and Naimark's theorem is used to relate POVMs to projective measurements. A quantum circuit is constructed for cyclic-group harmonic frames using a Fourier matrix and a permutation matrix.
AI.result: A necessary and sufficient condition for separability of harmonic frames is derived from the abelian group structure theorem. A necessary condition on subsystem dimensions for maximum entanglement in bipartite systems is obtained. A quantum circuit implementing harmonic frames for cyclic groups as POVMs is constructed using Fourier and permutation matrices, with simple examples applied to quantum computers.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of harmonic frames in terms of abelian group structure, yielding separability and entanglement criteria, and demonstrates practical quantum circuit implementations for cyclic-group harmonic frames, with suggestions for future work to improve circuit design and extend to all harmonic frames.

title: Is the H Atom Surrounded by A Cloud of Virtual Quanta Due to the Lamb Shift?
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, Revised version submitted to arXiv 7/28/2026
summary:
\abstract{The Lamb shift, one of the most fundamental interactions in atomic physics, arises from the interaction of H atoms with the electromagnetic fluctuations of the quantum vacuum. The energy shift has been computed in a variety of ways. The energy shift, as Feynman and Power demonstrated, equals the change in the vacuum energy in the volume containing the H atoms due to the change in the index of refraction arising from the presence of the H atoms. By using this result and a group theoretical calculation of the contribution to the Lamb shift from each frequency of the vacuum fluctuations, we can obtain an expression for the size of the region of vacuum energy for each frequency \texorpdfstring{$ω$}{ω} around the H atom due to the Lamb shift. The ground state atom is surrounded by a region of positive vacuum energy that extends well beyond the atom for low frequencies. This region can be described as a steady state cloud of virtual quanta. For energies \texorpdfstring{$E=\hbarω$}{E=hbar omega} eV less than 1 eV, the radius of the positive energy region is approximately 14. 4/E Angstroms. For a vacuum fluctuation of wavelength \texorpdfstring{$λ$}{lambda} the radius is \texorpdfstring{$(α/2π)λ$}{(alpha/2pi) lambda}. Thus, for long wavelengths, the region has macroscopic dimensions. The energy-time Uncertainty Relation predicts a maximum possible radius that is larger than this by a factor of \texorpdfstring{$1/ 4α$}{1/(4 alpha)}.}
  \keyword{Bethe; radiative shift; shift spectral density; spectral volume; vacuum fluctuations; vacuum field; Lamb shift; QED; energy field, renormalization, zero point fluctuations; hydrogen atom}.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an expression for the spatial extent of vacuum energy surrounding a hydrogen atom in its ground state, arising from the Lamb shift. By combining Feynman and Power's result that the Lamb shift equals the change in vacuum energy due to the atom's altered index of refraction, with a group-theoretical calculation of the shift per frequency, the authors show the ground-state atom is surrounded by a positive vacuum-energy region with radius (α/2π)λ for a vacuum fluctuation of wavelength λ, approximately 14.4/E Å for photon energy E (in eV) below 1 eV. These regions can be macroscopic in size.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to provide a physical, spatial interpretation of the Lamb shift by determining the size of the vacuum-energy region around a hydrogen atom contributed by each frequency of vacuum fluctuations, thereby illuminating the nature of the quantum vacuum's interaction with matter.
AI.method: The authors use the established result (due to Feynman and Power) that the Lamb shift energy equals the change in vacuum energy in the volume containing the H atoms, arising from the change in refractive index caused by the atoms. They combine this with a group-theoretical calculation that decomposes the Lamb shift contribution per frequency ω of vacuum fluctuations, enabling the derivation of a frequency-dependent radius of the vacuum-energy region around the atom.
AI.result: The ground-state hydrogen atom is surrounded by a positive vacuum-energy region that, for low frequencies, extends well beyond the atom and can be described as a steady-state cloud of virtual quanta. For photon energy E < 1 eV, the radius is approximately 14.4/E Å, and for a vacuum fluctuation of wavelength λ, the radius is (α/2π)λ, giving macroscopic dimensions for long wavelengths. The energy-time uncertainty relation yields a maximum possible radius larger by a factor of 1/(4α) ≈ 34.
AI.conclusion: The spatial footprint of the Lamb shift in the quantum vacuum is frequency-dependent and can extend to macroscopic scales for low-frequency vacuum fluctuations, with the energy-time uncertainty principle permitting an even larger limiting radius. This provides a physically intuitive picture of the vacuum-energy cloud surrounding the hydrogen atom.

title: LLM-Guided Initialization for Accelerated Hybrid Quantum-Classical Medical Image Classification
summary: Variational quantum algorithms often encounter barren plateaus, where cost gradients decay rapidly with increasing circuit depth, undermining the trainability of parameterized quantum circuits. This paper evaluates AdaInit (Adaptive Initialization), proposed by Zhuang and Cunningham, which uses large language models to propose initial parameters for quantum neural networks. We study a simplified single-query AdaInit variant paired with GPU-accelerated simulation in NVIDIA CUDA-Q and apply it to binary classification on the DMR-IR mammography dataset. AdaInit delivers 14.6 times higher gradient variance at initialization than random initialization (0.0095 vs. 0.0006), producing 160 times faster convergence (1.1s vs. 176 s) while maintaining the same classification accuracy of 61.4 percent. We provide theoretical analysis grounded in the geometry of parameterized circuit landscapes and show empirically that LLM-guided initialization places the optimizer in trainable regions of parameter space. Beyond performance, our results indicate that a single LLM query can yield informative parameters without iterative refinement, suggesting a low-overhead path to improved trainability. The findings validate AdaInit in a medical imaging setting and demonstrate its compatibility with GPU-accelerated quantum backends for practical speedups.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates AdaInit, an LLM-based adaptive initialization strategy for variational quantum circuits, using a simplified single-query variant on NVIDIA CUDA-Q GPU-accelerated simulation. Applied to binary classification on the DMR-IR mammography dataset, AdaInit achieves 14.6x higher gradient variance, 160x faster convergence, and equal accuracy (61.4%) compared to random initialization, with theoretical grounding in parameterized circuit landscape geometry.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from barren plateaus where cost gradients decay exponentially with circuit depth, severely limiting trainability. The authors aim to address this by evaluating whether LLM-guided parameter initialization can place quantum circuits in trainable regions of parameter space, thereby mitigating barren plateau effects.
AI.method: The paper evaluates a simplified single-query variant of AdaInit (Adaptive Initialization) that uses large language models to propose initial parameters for quantum neural networks. It is paired with GPU-accelerated simulation in NVIDIA CUDA-Q and applied to binary classification on the DMR-IR mammography dataset. The approach is validated through empirical comparison against random initialization and supported by theoretical analysis based on the geometry of parameterized circuit landscapes.
AI.result: AdaInit delivers 14.6 times higher gradient variance at initialization (0.0095 vs. 0.0006), 160 times faster convergence (1.1s vs. 176s), while maintaining identical classification accuracy of 61.4%. A single LLM query yields informative parameters without needing iterative refinement.
AI.conclusion: LLM-guided initialization effectively mitigates barren plateaus by positioning optimizers in trainable regions of parameter space. AdaInit is validated in a medical imaging context and demonstrates compatibility with GPU-accelerated quantum backends, offering a low-overhead, practical path to improved trainability in variational quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum State Discrimination With Stabilizer Circuits
summary: The task of quantum state discrimination provides an operational characterization of distinguishability and plays a central role in quantum information science. Since the achievable success probability in quantum state discrimination depends both on the states being discriminated and on the allowed measurements, it is natural to study discrimination under physically motivated measurement constraints. Here, we investigate minimum-error quantum state discrimination under measurements implementable by both fixed and adaptive stabilizer circuits. Given arbitrary stabilizer-state ancillas, we show that fixed stabilizer circuits provide no additional discrimination power, whereas adaptive circuits do. Then, focusing on single-qubit systems, we derive analytical expressions for the success probability across both circuit classes when supplied with arbitrary (non-stabilizer) ancillas, showing that the performance gap between fixed and adaptive circuits persists. We further consider discrimination with non-stabilizerness incorporated directly into the measurement operators. Here, the optimization is formulated as a semidefinite program, and analytical bounds interpolating between the stabilizer and Helstrom limits for qubits are derived. Finally, we illustrate applications in quantum random access codes and bounds on unitary synthesis fidelity with a finite number of magic states.

AI.tldr: This paper studies minimum-error quantum state discrimination under measurements constrained to stabilizer circuits (both fixed and adaptive). It shows fixed stabilizer circuits provide no additional discrimination power beyond without them, while adaptive circuits do. For single-qubit systems, analytical expressions for success probability are derived across both circuit classes with arbitrary ancillas. The paper also formulates discrimination with non-stabilizerness (magic) in measurement operators as a semidefinite program and derives analytical bounds interpolating between stabilizer and Helstrom limits for qubits, with applications to quantum random access codes and unitary synthesis fidelity with finite magic states.
AI.motivation: Quantum state discrimination is central to quantum information science, and the achievable success probability depends on the allowed measurements. Understanding how physically motivated measurement constraints—specifically those from stabilizer circuits—affect discrimination power is important since such circuits are experimentally feasible. This paper aims to characterize the discrimination capability of stabilizer-based measurements and the role of non-stabilizerness (magic) in enhancing discrimination performance.
AI.method: The authors (1) analyze fixed and adaptive stabilizer circuit measurements with stabilizer-state ancillas, showing fixed circuits offer no additional discrimination power while adaptive ones do; (2) derive analytical expressions for single-qubit success probabilities for both circuit classes with arbitrary (non-stabilizer) ancillas; (3) formulate discrimination with non-stabilizerness in measurement operators as a semidefinite program; and (4) derive analytical bounds interpolating between stabilizer and Helstrom limits for qubit systems.
AI.result: Fixed stabilizer circuits with stabilizer ancillas do not enhance discrimination power, whereas adaptive stabilizer circuits do. For single-qubit systems with arbitrary ancillas, the performance gap between fixed and adaptive circuits persists. With non-stabilizerness incorporated into measurement operators, the problem becomes a semidefinite program with analytical bounds interpolating between the stabilizer and Helstrom limits for qubits. Applications include quantum random access codes and bounds on unitary synthesis fidelity with a finite number of magic states.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive characterization of quantum state discrimination under stabilizer measurement constraints, establishing a clear hierarchy in discrimination power between fixed and adaptive stabilizer circuits, and quantifying how non-stabilizerness (magic) resources improve discrimination performance. The derived bounds and semi-definite programming formulation have practical implications for quantum random access codes and magic-state-based unitary synthesis.

title: Quantum vs Classical Erasure: Equal Bounds but Unequal Costs
summary: Irreversibility has a fundamental thermodynamic cost, erasing information inevitably generates heat. This connection is quantified by the Landauer bound, which gives the minimum dissipation needed to erase a single bit of information. While this bound applies in both classical and quantum settings, it is saturated only in idealised limits of infinite resources. Here, we provide a unified first principles description of finite-resource erasure in both classical and quantum systems. We begin by proving the communal folklore that in the idealised regime the erasure cost of a bit encoded in a quantum or classical system is the same. Despite this, we show that their practical implementation differs substantially: achieving comparable erasure quality in quantum systems requires more control, larger accessible energy gaps and longer operation times. Classical protocols can achieve the erasure of a comparable quantum protocol under far weaker constraints which we expose in trade-off relations. Our results explain why practical erasure schemes fall short of Landauer's bound and show that classical systems enjoy several fundamental thermodynamic advantages.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a unified first-principles framework for finite-resource information erasure in both classical and quantum systems. It proves that while the idealized erasure cost is identical for both (saturating the Landauer bound), practical implementations differ greatly: quantum erasure demands more control, larger energy gaps, and longer times, whereas classical protocols achieve comparable quality under far weaker constraints, revealing fundamental thermodynamic advantages of classical systems.
AI.motivation: The Landauer bound sets the minimum thermodynamic cost of erasing one bit of information, but it is only saturated in idealised limits with infinite resources. Practical erasure schemes always fall short of this bound, and a unified, first-principles understanding of how finite resources affect erasure in both classical and quantum settings has been lacking. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors derive a unified first-principles description of finite-resource erasure applicable to both classical and quantum systems. They prove that the idealized erasure cost is the same regardless of whether the bit is encoded in a classical or quantum system. They then analyze the practical resource requirements for achieving comparable erasure quality, deriving explicit trade-off relations that expose the minimal control, energy gap, and operation time needed in each setting.
AI.result: They prove that in the idealized regime, classical and quantum erasure costs coincide. However, practical implementations differ substantially: quantum erasure requires more control, larger accessible energy gaps, and longer operation times to achieve erasure quality comparable to classical protocols. They derive trade-off relations showing classical protocols can perform comparable erasure under far weaker constraints.
AI.conclusion: The results explain why practical erasure schemes fall short of the Landauer bound and demonstrate that classical systems possess several fundamental thermodynamic advantages over quantum systems in the context of finite-resource information erasure.

title: Restrictions on non-Clifford fault tolerance and ruling out beyond-SQL quantum metrology
summary: Quantum metrology promises a quadratic speedup over the standard quantum limit (SQL), but signal-aligned noise is expected to preclude this advantage in realistic settings. A potential route around known no-go results is to encode the sensors in a quantum code where the physical signal acts transversally as a logical gate. Understanding restrictions on transversal non-Clifford gates is therefore central to both quantum metrology and fault-tolerant quantum computation. Here, we prove such restrictions and apply them to transversal sensing. For any stabilizer code of distance $d\ge 3$ supporting a transversal logical action in level $D$ of the Clifford hierarchy, every stabilizer generating set must contain a check of weight at least $2^D$. Moreover, any $r$-level concatenated realization satisfies $r\leq \lfloor \log_2 n/D\rfloor$, forcing $r=1$ and ruling out concatenation when applied to beyond-SQL metrology. We then show that transversal single-qubit rotations by a small angle $θ$ can only induce a nontrivial logical action on an $n$-qubit code if its checks include irreducible stabilizers of weight $Ω(1/(n|θ|^2))$. Here, many single-qubit errors commute with every stabilizer or logical Pauli below this weight and are only detected by a high-weight check, so their syndromes cannot be fault-tolerantly reconstructed from low-weight normalizer measurements. Since beyond-SQL transversal sensing requires $|θ| = o(n^{-1/2})$, the weight of checks required for syndrome extraction diverges with $n$. Finally, we prove a broader metrological no-go theorem that avoids the assumptions of the quantum Cramér-Rao bound: constant-strength signal-aligned noise rules out any asymptotic advantage over the SQL in AC or DC sensing, even with biased estimators, nonstabilizer or approximate encodings, quantum memory, intermediate measurements, or adaptive control.

AI.tldr: This paper proves fundamental restrictions on transversal non-Clifford gates in stabilizer codes and applies them to quantum metrology. The authors show that distance-3 stabilizer codes supporting transversal logical gates in level D of the Clifford hierarchy must have checks of weight at least 2^D, and concatenation is ruled out for beyond-SQL metrology. They additionally prove that small-angle transversal rotations require high-weight checks for syndrome extraction, and establish a broad no-go theorem showing constant-strength signal-aligned noise precludes any asymptotic advantage over the SQL in AC or DC sensing under very general conditions.
AI.motivation: Quantum metrology using transversal encodings promises a quadratic speedup over the standard quantum limit, but signal-aligned noise is expected to nullify this advantage. To understand whether encoding sensors in quantum codes with transversal logical gates can circumvent known no-go results, the authors need to characterize fundamental restrictions on transversal non-Clifford gates—a question central to both quantum metrology and fault-tolerant quantum computation.
AI.method: The authors prove structural theorems about stabilizer codes: (1) any stabilizer code of distance d≥3 supporting transversal logical action at level D of the Clifford hierarchy must have a check of weight ≥2^D; (2) any r-level concatenated realization satisfies r ≤ ⌊log₂ n/D⌋, forcing r=1 for beyond-SQL metrology; (3) small-angle transversal rotations θ induce nontrivial logical actions only if checks include irreducible stabilizers of weight Ω(1/(n|θ|²)), meaning syndrome extraction requires high-weight measurements that cannot be fault-tolerantly reconstructed; (4) a broad no-go theorem is proven that avoids quantum Cramér-Rao bound assumptions, covering AC/DC sensing with biased estimators, nonstabilizer or approximate encodings, quantum memory, intermediate measurements, and adaptive control under constant-strength signal-aligned noise.
AI.result: The paper proves that transversal non-Clifford gates in stabilizer codes impose strict weight constraints on stabilizer checks: at least 2^D for level-D Clifford hierarchy actions. Concatenation is impossible for beyond-SQL metrology (r=1 forced). For small-angle rotations θ, syndrome extraction requires high-weight checks whose weights diverge with n when |θ| = o(n^{-1/2}) as required for beyond-SQL sensing. Finally, a general no-go theorem rules out any asymptotic advantage over the SQL under constant-strength signal-aligned noise in both AC and DC sensing, removing reliance on Cramér-Rao bound assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The results close the loophole of using transversal non-Clifford encodings for beyond-standard-quantum-limit metrology. The structural weight bounds on stabilizer checks needed for transversal non-Clifford gates, combined with the fault-tolerant syndrome extraction requirements, make such sensing schemes impractical or impossible. The broad no-go theorem decisively establishes that constant-strength signal-aligned noise precludes any asymptotic quantum advantage over the SQL in realistic sensing scenarios.

title: Area-Information Trade-Offs in Acceleration Radiation from Atoms Falling into Black Holes
summary: We develop a geometric theory of information processing in the Horizon-brightened acceleration radiation (HBAR) channel, in which the radiative horizon-area change provides an entropy budget for the information carried by the radiation field. Building on the quantum-optical description of atom--field interactions near the horizon and the resulting HBAR thermodynamic correspondence, we derive area-cost laws in the near-steady, thermally saturated regime. The accessible classical information and the mutual information generated between the radiation field and its environment are bounded by the associated radiative horizon-area budget. Reliability is incorporated through Fano's inequality, which translates a prescribed decoding error probability into an area requirement. We further derive Fisher-information speed limits that constrain the statistical evolution of the radiation field and place a lower bound on the duration required for correlation generation. Together, these results establish a bits-per-area principle linking black-hole thermodynamics, information geometry, and quantum information in the HBAR framework.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a geometric theory of information processing in the Horizon-brightened acceleration radiation (HBAR) channel, deriving area-cost laws, information bounds, and Fisher-information speed limits that establish a bits-per-area principle linking black-hole thermodynamics to information geometry and quantum information.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous geometric framework for quantifying information processing in the HBAR channel, where radiative horizon-area change serves as an entropy budget, thereby connecting black-hole thermodynamics with information-theoretic bounds.
AI.method: The approach builds on quantum-optical descriptions of atom-field interactions near the horizon and the HBAR thermodynamic correspondence. Using area-cost laws in the near-steady thermally saturated regime, the authors bound accessible classical information and mutual information via radiative horizon-area budgets. Fano's inequality translates decoding error probabilities into area requirements, and Fisher-information speed limits constrain the statistical evolution of the radiation field.
AI.result: The analysis yields bounds on classical and mutual information in terms of radiative horizon-area budgets, area requirements derived from decoding error probabilities, and lower bounds on the duration for correlation generation via Fisher-information speed limits.
AI.conclusion: The results collectively establish a bits-per-area principle that unifies black-hole thermodynamics, information geometry, and quantum information within the HBAR framework.

title: Bosonic quantum communication beyond the thermal threshold
summary: The quantum capacity of the bosonic thermal attenuator, which is given by the regularization of its coherent information, is unknown. The seminal work of Holevo and Werner established in 1999 the standard one-use lower bound obtained from input thermal states. We first prove that this long-standing lower bound is the exact supremum over all single-mode Gaussian states and then show that, crucially, a non-Gaussian state can do better. As a consequence, we prove positivity of the quantum capacity in a parameter region where the channel is not antidegradable, yet its coherent information optimized over single-mode Gaussian states vanishes. For example, with one thermal photon in the environment and at transmissivity $η=0.8$, the coherent information is non-positive for every single-mode Gaussian input. We give an explicit rank-two non-Gaussian state, supported on only six Fock levels, whose coherent information is certified to be at least $4.7\times10^{-4}$ qubits per channel use. This short witness is far from numerically optimal: a numerical optimization over fixed non-Gaussian families reaches at least $8.4\times 10^{-3}$ qubits per channel use at the same point. More generally, at $ν=1$, using non-Gaussian inputs we certify positivity of the coherent information, and therefore of the quantum capacity, down to $η=0.7841$; by contrast, the channel is antidegradable, and hence has zero quantum capacity, for $η\leq0.75$. Overall, our work identifies new high-noise regimes in which bosonic quantum communication is possible.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the Holevo-Werner lower bound on the coherent information of the bosonic thermal attenuator is tight over all single-mode Gaussian states, but shows a non-Gaussian state can exceed it. This establishes positive quantum capacity in parameter regions where Gaussian-optimized coherent information vanishes and the channel is not antidegradable, e.g., at one thermal photon and transmissivity η=0.8, where a rank-two Fock-supported state achieves coherent information ≥4.7×10⁻⁴ qubits per use (numerically up to 8.4×10⁻³).
AI.motivation: The quantum capacity of the bosonic thermal attenuator was unknown, since it requires regularizing coherent information. The authors aim to determine whether the long-standing 1999 Holevo-Werner bound from input thermal states is optimal, and whether non-Gaussian inputs can improve upon it in high-noise regimes.
AI.method: The authors first prove that the Holevo-Werner lower bound is exactly the supremum of coherent information over all single-mode Gaussian input states. They then construct an explicit rank-two non-Gaussian state supported on six Fock levels and certify its coherent information via numerical methods, also performing numerical optimization over fixed non-Gaussian families.
AI.result: A non-Gaussian state beats the Gaussian-optimized coherent information. At one thermal photon (ν=1) and η=0.8, the Gaussian-optimized coherent information is non-positive, but the explicit rank-two state achieves ≥4.7×10⁻⁴ qubits/use (certified), and numerical optimization reaches ≥8.4×10⁻³ qubits/use. Positivity of coherent information (and thus quantum capacity) is certified down to η=0.7841, above the antidegradable threshold η≤0.75 where capacity is zero.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies new high-noise regimes where bosonic quantum communication is possible via non-Gaussian inputs, disproving the optimality of Gaussian states for coherent information in these channels and providing the first certified positive quantum capacity in regions where Gaussian-optimized coherent information vanishes but the channel is not antidegradable.

title: Coherent excitation of a two-state system by a Lorentzian field
summary: We study the coherent excitation of a two-state quantum system by a field with a Lorentzian temporal envelope and constant carrier frequency. The associated differential equation admits an exact local representation in terms of confluent Heun functions. For the transition probability we develop a Dykhne-Davis-Pechukas (DDP) description based on the two relevant complex transition points and their interference. The DDP action is analyzed directly in the weak- and strong-coupling limits, yielding explicit asymptotic expressions for the oscillation phase, oscillation envelope, far-detuned line shape, and near-resonant behavior. In particular, the strong-coupling asymptotics imply a linewidth proportional to the inverse peak Rabi frequency for resonant odd-$π$ pulses, thereby exhibiting the power-narrowing characteristic of the Lorentzian pulse.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes coherent excitation of a two-state quantum system by a Lorentzian temporal envelope pulse at constant carrier frequency. The transition probability is described via Dykhne-Davis-Pechukas (DDP) theory based on interference of two complex transition points. Explicit asymptotic expressions are derived for weak- and strong-coupling limits, revealing power-narrowing behavior with a linewidth inversely proportional to the peak Rabi frequency for resonant odd-π pulses.
AI.motivation: To provide an exact and analytically tractable description of coherent two-state excitation driven by a Lorentzian-shaped pulse, extending DDP theory to this envelope and deriving explicit asymptotic formulas for observables such as line shape, oscillation phase, and linewidth.
AI.method: The Schrödinger equation for a two-state system driven by a Lorentzian-envelope field is solved using confluent Heun functions. The transition probability is then analyzed within the DDP framework using the two relevant complex transition points and their interference. Asymptotic analyses are performed in the weak- and strong-coupling limits.
AI.result: Explicit asymptotic expressions are obtained for the oscillation phase, oscillation envelope, far-detuned line shape, and near-resonant behavior in both weak- and strong-coupling regimes. For resonant odd-π pulses in the strong-coupling limit, the linewidth scales as the inverse peak Rabi frequency, demonstrating power-narrowing characteristic of the Lorentzian pulse.
AI.conclusion: The Lorentzian pulse envelope exhibits distinctive power-narrowing behavior, where increasing pulse strength narrows the resonance linewidth. The DDP framework, supported by exact Heun-function solutions, provides a complete quantitative description of the excitation dynamics across coupling regimes.

title: Closed Timelike Curve Decoding on Quantum Hardware
summary: Deutsch closed timelike curves (D-CTCs) are described by a fixed-point condition for a chronology-violating register. We study a finite-dimensional circuit model that places a Hayden--Preskill/Yoshida--Kitaev recovery map inside such a consistency loop. A register-routing construction makes the Deutsch map explicit: an initial SWAP moves the incoming CTC state to an idle dump register, the scrambler and decoder act on the remaining active registers, and a final SWAP writes the recovered message back to the CTC register. When the active branch recovers the message, the induced map on the CTC register is the replacement channel \(σ\mapsto ρ_M\), with the unique fixed point \(ρ_M\). We implement the associated Lloyd-type post-selected decoder circuits on quantum hardware and formulate a classical-feedback iteration for the experimentally estimated map. Qiskit simulations and IBM-hardware data for single-qubit instances quantify decoder fidelity, post-selection overhead, routing-dependent noise, and quantum-geometric susceptibility.

A register-routing construction makes the Deutsch map explicit, and when the active branch successfully recovers a message, the induced map on the CTC register becomes a replacement channel with a unique fixed point. The authors implement Lloyd-type post-selected decoder circuits on quantum hardware and use classical-feedback iteration on IBM hardware and Qiskit simulations for single-qubit instances, quantifying decoder fidelity, post-selection overhead, routing noise, and geometric susceptibility.

AI.method: A finite-dimensional circuit model places a recovery map inside a D-CTC consistency loop. A register-routing construction makes the Deutsch map explicit: an initial SWAP moves the incoming CTC state to an idle dump register, a scrambler and decoder act on active registers, and a final SWAP writes the recovered message back to the CTC register. title: Quantum Interference as a Proposal Mechanism for Combinatorial Optimization
comment: Main article with Supplementary Information; 5 main figures and 34 supplementary figures
summary: Quantum Interference Proposal Search (QIPS) uses seed-conditioned quantum circuits to generate localized interference patterns as finite-shot proposal distributions for QUBO/Ising optimization. Candidate $n_b$-bit strings are sampled from these distributions, scored classically and used to update an elite frontier of low-energy solutions. QIPS uses a fixed two-layer gate-based circuit architecture with 100 shots per circuit while the Hilbert-space dimension grows as $2^{n_b}$. Across six benchmark families with $18 \le n_b \le 29$, QIPS maintains competitive progress relative to a matched classical control that preserves the same search loop, frontier update rule and proposal budget, with total proposals proportional to $n_b$. Performance is assessed using top-$K$ coverage, hit rate, multiplicity, Hilbert-space coverage and dyadic-rank metrics. The results identify localized quantum interference as a resource-efficient proposal mechanism for computational quantum optimization.

Across six benchmark families (18 ≤ n_b ≤ 29), QIPS achieves competitive performance against a matched classical control with identical search loop and proposal budget, identifying localized quantum interference as a resource-efficient proposal mechanism for quantum optimization.

AI.method: QIPS generates proposal distributions via seed-conditioned quantum circuits with a fixed two-layer gate-based architecture, taking 100 shots per circuit. title: Floquet Abelian Multicycle Codes
summary: Abelian multicycle (AMC) codes are compact quantum low-density parity-check codes whose multiblock chain-complex structure provides redundant low-weight stabilizers and supports single-shot error correction. We introduce Floquet AMC codes by deriving a quotient-lattice representation of a general level-$j$, $D$-dimensional AMC complex over a finite Abelian group algebra, lifting this lattice to spacetime, and rotating the circuit-time direction in the associated ZX network. When the check and data spiders have even valence and admit a time-oriented local port matching, the network decomposes into a periodic schedule of native two-qubit $XX$ and $ZZ$ measurements. We construct generalized-bicycle and level-$2$ AMC4 examples, determine their instantaneous stabilizer groups, and compute their embedded distances by minimizing over all inequivalent circuit cuts. For AMC4 instances locally equivalent to four-dimensional toric codes, we obtain Floquet memories with parameters $[[108,6,5]]$, $[[144,6,8]]$, and $[[324,6,10]]$. Local Pauli-web detector templates and beam-search decoding under the measurement-native EM3 noise model yield an estimated pseudothreshold of approximately $1.2\%$. These results provide compact measurement-only realizations of higher-dimensional homological redundancy without directly measuring the original weight-six stabilizers.

By deriving a quotient-lattice representation of AMC complexes, lifting them to spacetime, and rotating the circuit-time direction in ZX networks, the authors create periodic schedules of native two-qubit XX/ZZ measurements. They construct concrete generalized-bicycle and AMC4 examples with parameters [[108,6,5]], [[144,6,8]], and [[324,6,10]], and demonstrate a pseudothreshold of ~1.2% under EM3 noise via beam-search decoding.
AI.motivation: Abelian multicycle (AMC) codes offer compact quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with redundant low-weight stabilizers and single-shot error correction, but they require directly measuring weight-six stabilizers, which is impractical. The authors aim to achieve measurement-only, hardware-native realizations of these higher-dimensional homological codes without such expensive stabilizer measurements.
