The demonstrated pseudothreshold of ~1.2% under a realistic measurement-native noise model indicates these codes are promising candidates for practical fault-tolerant quantum memories.

title: Noise-resilient and Scalable Quantum Error Correction for Nuclear Spin Qubits in Silicon with Electron Shuttling
summary: Nuclear spin qubits in silicon are well-isolated from their environment. Consequently, they have very long lifetimes and low sensitivity to noise, but this also suggests that control and measurement is challenging. We introduce electron pair interferometry (EPI), a protocol to overcome this challenge and maintain robustness to noise. EPI is implemented using an array of quantum dots with isoelectronic nuclear spin qubits located in the dots. A pair of electrons are initialized into a singlet ground state, split apart, and shuttled to the dots containing nuclear spin qubits. We show it is possible to coherently transfer the parity of the nuclei onto the measurable state of singlet/triplet-encoded electrons. Global nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) can be used to change bases and implement dynamical decoupling (DD). Combined with selective hyperfine-induced $Z_π$ rotations, our gate set is complete for universal quantum computation, tailored to Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error correction, and robust to noise. We discuss very low sensitivity to charge noise and study the sensitivity to both DC and AC magnetic field inhomogeneity which depends strongly on their relative strengths.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces electron pair interferometry (EPI), a protocol for controlling and measuring nuclear spin qubits in silicon quantum dots using pairs of electrons in singlet/triplet states. The protocol enables coherent transfer of nuclear parity onto measurable electron states, uses global NMR for dynamical decoupling, and achieves a universal, noise-robust gate set tailored to CSS quantum error correction.
AI.motivation: Nuclear spin qubits in silicon have exceptional coherence times but are extremely difficult to control and measure due to their strong isolation from the environment. This isolation makes readout and manipulation challenging, motivating a protocol that can reliably access these qubits while preserving their noise robustness.
AI.method: EPI uses an array of quantum dots containing isoelectronic nuclear spin qubits. Pairs of electrons are initialized into a singlet ground state, split and shuttled to dots holding the nuclear spins. The parity of the nuclei is coherently transferred onto the singlet/triplet state of the electron pair, enabling measurement. Global NMR pulses provide basis changes and dynamical decoupling, while selective hyperfine-induced Z_π rotations complete the gate set.
AI.result: The protocol achieves a complete gate set for universal quantum computation tailored to CSS quantum error correction. It demonstrates very low sensitivity to charge noise, and the sensitivity to DC and AC magnetic field inhomogeneity is analyzed, showing strong dependence on the relative strengths of these field inhomogeneities.
AI.conclusion: Electron pair interferometry provides a viable route to control and measure otherwise highly isolated nuclear spin qubits in silicon, maintaining robustness to noise while enabling universal quantum computation.

title: Efficient learning of bosonic unitaries beyond the Gaussian class
summary: Multimode quantum processes are generally difficult to learn, due to the large dimensionality and complex entanglement structure beyond the Gaussian class. Here, we show that the fundamental obstruction is not non-Gaussianity itself, but the buildup of irreducible multimode non-Gaussian correlations. We establish a tractability frontier for bosonic unitary learning: a general $m$-mode unitary with input energy at most $E$ per mode requires at least $Ω(E^{2m})$ channel uses, whereas two broad non-Gaussian families---$t$-doped Gaussian unitaries and Gaussian-entanglable unitaries---can be learned with resources polynomial in $m$. The latter can exhibit both extensive non-Gaussianity and strong multimode entanglement. Our forward-only protocols use coherent-state probes, Gaussian operations, local heterodyne detection, and classical post-processing to identify the global Gaussian mixing and reduce the remaining task to single- or few-mode learning. The analysis also yields a multimode quantum Darmois--Skitovich theorem showing that mode-spreading passive networks preserve product structure only for Gaussian input states, an almost-sure activation theorem for non-Gaussian processes showing that non-Gaussian unitaries yield non-Gaussian outputs for almost all coherent input states, and a method for learning unitaries from uncalibrated coherent probes. Our results identify that complexity of learning arises from irreducible mixing of non-Gaussianity and entanglement, rather than either resource alone.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a tractability frontier for multimode bosonic unitary learning, showing that the hardness of learning is fundamentally tied to irreducible multimode non-Gaussian correlations rather than non-Gaussianity alone. It proves a lower bound of Ω(E^{2m}) channel uses for general m-mode unitaries with per-mode energy E, while demonstrating that two broad non-Gaussian families—t-doped Gaussian unitaries and Gaussian-entanglable unitaries—can be learned with polynomial-in-m resources using forward-only protocols based on coherent-state probes, Gaussian operations, and local heterodyne detection.
AI.motivation: Multimode quantum processes are notoriously difficult to learn due to high dimensionality and complex entanglement structures beyond the Gaussian class. The authors aim to pinpoint the fundamental obstruction to efficient learning and characterize precisely when multimode bosonic unitary learning is tractable versus intractable.
AI.method: The authors establish rigorous complexity bounds: a general lower bound of Ω(E^{2m}) channel uses for arbitrary m-mode unitaries with per-mode energy E. They then design forward-only learning protocols for two non-Gaussian families using coherent-state probes, Gaussian operations, local heterodyne detection, and classical post-processing. The protocols first identify global Gaussian mixing, then reduce learning to single- or few-mode tasks. The analysis also develops a multimode quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem, an almost-sure activation theorem for non-Gaussian processes, and a technique for learning from uncalibrated coherent probes.
AI.result: The paper delineates a clear tractability frontier: general multimode unitaries require exponentially many channel uses in m, yet t-doped Gaussian unitaries and Gaussian-entanglable unitaries—which can exhibit both extensive non-Gaussianity and strong multimode entanglement—are efficiently learnable with polynomial resources. The supporting theorems provide structural insights into when non-Gaussianity activates and when product structure is preserved under passive networks.
AI.conclusion: The complexity of learning multimode quantum processes arises from the irreducible mixing of non-Gaussianity with entanglement, not from either resource in isolation. This reframes the learnability problem and provides both fundamental limits and efficient strategies for significant non-Gaussian families.

title: Exploring the use of quantum computing for facilitating spatially and temporally resolved models of a biological cell
summary: Whole-cell simulation, modeling all of a cell's functional systems over its life cycle, is an outstanding challenge in computational biology. Even the simplest living cell contains thousands of interacting proteins and metabolites (on the order of trillions of atoms) whose full functional dynamics spans roughly five orders of magnitude in space (nm to $μ$m) and nearly nineteen in time (fs to hours). Further, many of the governing physical and chemical properties remain incompletely characterized. Simulating such complex systems at fully atomistic resolution over a full cell cycle is computationally intractable on classical architectures, raising a central question: Can quantum computing offer a viable path to whole-cell simulations that integrate molecular- and systems-level complexity? This Perspective examines the potential of quantum computing across three hierarchical scales: atomistic-molecular modeling, metabolic and regulatory networks, and whole-cell spatial modeling. We present a complexity analysis comparing classical and quantum algorithms for representative biological problems, identifying regimes of substantial theoretical speedup under specified algorithmic assumptions. We highlight algorithmic developments designed to leverage both near-term exploratory and fault-tolerant quantum architectures, and discuss practical bottlenecks: data encoding overhead, system conditioning, measurement constraints, and hybrid quantum-HPC integration. Together, these results outline a roadmap for quantum-accelerated whole-cell modeling and the biological insights such multiscale frameworks may eventually enable.

AI.tldr: This Perspective examines whether quantum computing can enable whole-cell simulation - a computationally intractable challenge on classical architectures - by analyzing quantum algorithm potential across three hierarchical scales (atomistic-molecular, metabolic/regulatory networks, and whole-cell spatial modeling), identifying theoretical speedup regimes, and outlining a roadmap for quantum-accelerated whole-cell modeling.
AI.motivation: Whole-cell simulation is a grand challenge in computational biology: even the simplest cell contains thousands of interacting proteins and metabolites spanning ~5 orders of magnitude in space and ~19 in time, yet full atomistic resolution over a cell cycle is intractable on classical machines. The paper motivates the central question of whether quantum computing can offer a viable pathway to bridge molecular- and systems-level complexity for whole-cell modeling.
AI.method: The paper presents a Perspective-based analysis across three hierarchical scales (atomistic-molecular modeling, metabolic and regulatory networks, and whole-cell spatial modeling). It provides complexity analyses comparing classical versus quantum algorithms for representative biological problems, identifies theoretical speedup regimes under specified algorithmic assumptions, and highlights algorithmic developments targeting both near-term exploratory (NISQ) and fault-tolerant quantum architectures, along with discussion of practical bottlenecks including data encoding overhead, system conditioning, measurement constraints, and hybrid quantum-HPC integration.
AI.result: The analysis identifies regimes of substantial theoretical speedup for quantum algorithms on representative biological problems under stated assumptions. It describes algorithmic strategies suited to both near-term and fault-tolerant quantum hardware, and enumerates practical bottlenecks (data encoding, conditioning, measurement, hybrid HPC integration) that must be addressed, collectively outlining a roadmap for quantum-accelerated whole-cell modeling.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that quantum computing offers a plausible, though non-trivial, path toward whole-cell simulation, outlining a roadmap that integrates multiscale modeling with quantum algorithms. It suggests such quantum-accelerated frameworks may eventually enable biological insights that are currently unattainable with classical computing alone.

title: Quantum LDPC codes with design rate 1/5 and good performance below 1000 physical qubits
summary: Constant-rate quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes promise fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant spatial overhead in the asymptotic limit. Nonetheless, discovering finite-length code instances with good practical performance remains challenging. We introduce a new family of quantum LDPC codes with design rate $1/5$ and check weight $9$ that approaches the teraquop memory regime per qubit-round with several hundred physical qubits, under idling-free circuit-level noise of strength $0.1\%$ and GPU-accelerated Relay-belief-propagation (Relay-BP) decoding with average latencies around 1-2 ms, a regime relevant to trapped-ion and neutral-atom processors. The construction involves the balanced product of classical LDPC codes with design rate $1/2$ that share non-abelian $\mathbb{Z}_\ell \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_m$ group symmetries, which may be of independent interest for classical error correction. We build syndrome extraction circuits tailored to reconfigurable atom arrays using a simple greedy scheduler, with single-round rearrangement times around 30-60 ms using present hardware specifications, and substantial room for future improvements. We also construct logical Pauli bases that are equivariant with respect to the group symmetry, which can significantly compress the design space for code surgery. Together, these results further advance the practicality of constant-rate quantum LDPC codes for near-term, fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new family of quantum LDPC codes with design rate 1/5 and check weight 9, constructed via balanced products of classical LDPC codes with non-abelian group symmetries. The codes achieve teraquop-level memory performance per qubit-round with a few hundred physical qubits under circuit-level noise, enabled by GPU-accelerated Relay-BP decoding, and include practical syndrome extraction circuits designed for reconfigurable atom arrays.
AI.motivation: Constant-rate quantum LDPC codes promise asymptotically constant spatial overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but discovering finite-length code instances with good practical performance remains difficult. The authors aim to bridge the gap between theoretical asymptotic promises and practical code instances suitable for near-term fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
AI.method: The codes are constructed via the balanced product of classical LDPC codes with design rate 1/2 that share non-abelian Z_l ⋊ Z_m group symmetries. The authors build syndrome extraction circuits tailored to reconfigurable atom arrays using a simple greedy scheduler, and construct logical Pauli bases equivariant with respect to the group symmetry to compress the design space for code surgery. Decoding uses GPU-accelerated Relay belief-propagation.
AI.result: The codes approach the teraquop memory regime per qubit-round with several hundred physical qubits under idling-free circuit-level noise of 0.1%, with decoding latencies around 1-2 ms. Single-round rearrangement times for atom arrays are estimated at 30-60 ms with present hardware, showing substantial room for improvement.
AI.conclusion: The results advance the practicality of constant-rate quantum LDPC codes for near-term fault-tolerant quantum computing, particularly in trapped-ion and neutral-atom processor contexts, by providing finite-length code instances with competitive performance and hardware-tailored circuit implementations.

title: Quadruply Bonded Mo2 Molecules: An Innate Emitter-Resonator Quantum System in Free Space
summary: In recent decades, significant progress has been made in constructing and studying individual quantum systems based on two level atoms (molecules) and photons. Here we demonstrate that the quadruply bonded Mo2 unit, with a MoMo bond distance as short as 2.1A, functions as an innate emitter resonator molecular quantum system capable of trapping visible light photons between the two molybdenum atoms under ambient conditions, thereby generating an intense quantized local electromagnetic field with an extremely small mode volume. The resonance fluorescence spectra of three Mo2 complexes indicate that the intermetallic Mo-Mo charge transfer transition is coherently coupled to the local scattering field, exhibiting vacuum Rabi splitting and Mollow triplets. Resonant coupling of single molecules and N-molecule ensembles to the scattered light through sideband excitation produces a sequence of discrete optical modes spanning a broad wavelength range, with polaritonic transitions identical to those observed in Ni2 based systems. These results establish the Mo2 molecule as an independent emitter resonator integrated quantum system that enables quantum optical experiments in free space using conventional spectroscopic instrumentation. This work extends quantum electrodynamics into molecular science, providing new insights into metal metal bonding, molecular physics, and light matter interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that quadruply bonded Mo2 units act as innate emitter-resonator molecular quantum systems, trapping visible light photons between two molybdenum atoms at ambient conditions. The Mo-Mo charge transfer transition exhibits vacuum Rabi splitting and Mollow triplets, establishing the Mo2 molecule as an integrated quantum system that enables quantum optical experiments in free space using conventional spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: To extend quantum electrodynamics into molecular science by demonstrating that a simple molecular unit (the quadruply bonded Mo2 dimer) can function as an integrated emitter-resonator quantum system, eliminating the need for external optical cavities and enabling quantum optical experiments in free space with conventional instrumentation.
AI.method: The study employs resonance fluorescence spectroscopy on three Mo2 complexes with short Mo-Mo bond distances (~2.1 Å). The experimental approach examines the intermetallic Mo-Mo charge transfer transition and its coherent coupling to the local scattering field. Analysis includes single-molecule and N-molecule ensemble resonant coupling to scattered light via sideband excitation.
AI.result: The Mo2 unit traps visible photons between the two molybdenum atoms, generating an intense quantized local electromagnetic field with extremely small mode volume. The resonance fluorescence spectra exhibit vacuum Rabi splitting and Mollow triplets, confirming strong coupling. A sequence of discrete optical modes spanning a broad wavelength range is observed, with polaritonic transitions matching those in Ni2-based systems.
AI.conclusion: The Mo2 molecule constitutes an independent emitter-resonator integrated quantum system, enabling quantum optical experiments in free space without external cavities. This work extends quantum electrodynamics into molecular science and provides new insights into metal-metal bonding, molecular physics, and light-matter interactions.

title: Quantum coherence and entanglement in wireless quantum batteries
comment: 12 pages, 11 figures, comments are welcome. Accepted by Physical Review A
summary: We investigate the charging dynamics and thermodynamic performance of a wireless quantum battery system mediated by a common structured bosonic environment. By employing a unified resource-theoretic analysis, we elucidate the distinct roles of non-Markovian memory effects and coupling symmetry in regulating energy transfer. In the Markovian weak-coupling regime, we identify a transformative mechanism where the dynamic reconstruction of $l_1$-norm coherence compensates for the monotonic decay of first-order coherence to sustain energy transport. Conversely, the non-Markovian strong-coupling regime facilitates a cooperative resonance, characterized by the synchronized oscillation of entanglement and stored energy induced by environmental backflow. Furthermore, we reveal that coupling symmetry acts as a critical control parameter: while asymmetric coupling favoring the battery optimizes energy gain in memoryless environments, symmetric coupling under strong interactions unlocks a dark-state protection mechanism, effectively trapping energy within a decoherence-free subspace. Finally, a thermodynamic analysis based on ergotropy demonstrates that first-order coherence establishes the activation threshold for incoherent work, whereas $l_1$-norm coherence serves as the explicit fuel for coherent work extraction. These findings provide a refined theoretical framework for engineering environment-assisted quantum energy storage devices.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a wireless quantum battery system mediated by a structured bosonic environment, revealing how non-Markovian memory effects, coupling symmetry, and different coherence measures (l1-norm vs. first-order) govern energy transfer and work extraction in thermodynamics.
AI.motivation: To refine the theoretical framework for engineering environment-assisted quantum energy storage devices by understanding how environmental memory effects, coupling symmetry, and coherence types regulate energy transfer and thermodynamic performance in wireless quantum batteries.
AI.method: The authors employ a unified resource-theoretic analysis, investigating two regimes: (1) Markovian weak-coupling where dynamic reconstruction of l1-norm coherence compensates for monotonic decay of first-order coherence; (2) non-Markovian strong-coupling where cooperative resonance emerges via synchronized oscillation of entanglement and stored energy induced by environmental backflow. Coupling symmetry is analyzed as a control parameter, and ergotropy-based thermodynamic analysis distinguishes incoherent vs. coherent work extraction.
AI.result: Asymmetric coupling favoring the battery optimizes energy gain in memoryless environments, while symmetric coupling under strong interactions enables a dark-state protection mechanism that traps energy within a decoherence-free subspace. First-order coherence establishes the activation threshold for incoherent work, whereas l1-norm coherence acts as explicit fuel for coherent work extraction.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish that non-Markovianity, coupling symmetry, and distinct coherence types play complementary and tunable roles in quantum battery performance, providing a refined theoretical foundation for environment-assisted quantum energy storage engineering.

title: Phase Retrieval in $\mathbb C^4$ Requires Exactly Eleven Measurements
summary: Determining the minimal number of intensity measurements required for phase retrieval in $\mathbb{C}^4$ has been a long-standing open problem. Prior to this work, the best-known results implied that this minimum was either $10$ or $11$. In this paper, we leverage characteristic classes and cohomology groups from differential topology to prove that no family of $10$ vectors in $\mathbb{C}^4$ possesses the phase retrieval property. Combining our lower bound with Vinzant's explicit eleven-vector construction establishes that the exact minimum is $11$. Our result yields a significant consequence for pure state quantum tomography, namely, a rank-one POVM on $\mathbb{C}^4$ requires exactly $11$ elements to be informationally complete for pure states. This further implies that three orthonormal bases are insufficient to uniquely distinguish all pure states in $\mathbb{C}^4$. Because four orthonormal bases are already known to be sufficient, we conclude that exactly four bases are required, thereby completely resolving the problem left in [C. Carmeli, T. Heinosaari, J. Schultz, A. Toigo, Eur. Phys. J. D].

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the minimal number of intensity measurements required for phase retrieval in C^4 is exactly 11, resolving a long-standing open problem by using tools from differential topology (characteristic classes and cohomology groups). This confirms that no 10 vectors can have the phase retrieval property, and implies that a rank-one POVM on C^4 requires exactly 11 elements for pure state tomography, meaning exactly four orthonormal bases are needed.
AI.motivation: Determining the minimal number of intensity measurements for phase retrieval in C^4 was a long-standing open problem. Prior results only narrowed the answer to either 10 or 11, leaving a gap that needed to be closed.
AI.method: The authors apply techniques from differential topology, specifically characteristic classes and cohomology groups, to establish that no set of 10 vectors in C^4 can satisfy the phase retrieval property. They combine this lower bound with Vinzant's explicit construction of 11 vectors to establish the exact minimum.
AI.result: The exact minimum number of intensity measurements for phase retrieval in C^4 is proven to be 11. This also resolves that a rank-one POVM on C^4 requires exactly 11 elements to be informationally complete for pure states, and exactly four orthonormal bases are required (three are insufficient, four suffice).
AI.conclusion: The paper completely resolves the open problem of the minimal number of intensity measurements for phase retrieval in C^4, establishing the answer as 11, and thereby settles related questions in pure state quantum tomography, including the necessity of four orthonormal bases.

title: Exact Incompatibility-Breaking Criterion for Unital Qubit Channels
summary: We study when a noisy qubit channel renders all positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs) jointly measurable. For every unital qubit channel, we derive the exact incompatibility-breaking criterion and prove that projective measurements already determine the boundary for arbitrary POVMs. Through the steering--joint-measurability correspondence, this result gives the exact POVM-steering boundary for all two-qubit states with maximally mixed marginals, with the Werner states recovered as a special case. For nonunital qubit channels, we construct a generally asymmetric parent POVM and obtain an explicit sufficient incompatibility-breaking condition, which in turn yields a sufficient unsteerability criterion for arbitrary two-qubit states.

AI.tldr: This paper derives exact criteria for when noisy qubit channels break joint measurability of all POVMs. For unital qubit channels, an exact incompatibility-breaking criterion is found, with projective measurements determining the boundary for arbitrary POVMs. This gives exact POVM-steering boundaries for two-qubit states with maximally mixed marginals (including Werner states). For nonunital channels, a generally asymmetric parent POVM provides a sufficient incompatibility-breaking condition and a sufficient unsteerability criterion for arbitrary two-qubit states.
AI.motivation: To characterize when quantum channels destroy all measurement incompatibility (joint measurability of POVMs), which connects to quantum steering and foundational/operational questions about noisy quantum devices.
AI.method: For unital qubit channels, an exact incompatibility-breaking criterion is derived, and it is proven that projective measurements already determine the incompatibility-breaking boundary for arbitrary POVMs. The steering–joint-measurability correspondence is leveraged to translate findings into steering results. For nonunital channels, an asymmetric parent POVM is explicitly constructed to obtain a sufficient incompatibility-breaking condition.
AI.result: Exact incompatibility-breaking criteria for all unital qubit channels; exact POVM-steering boundaries for two-qubit states with maximally mixed marginals (Werner states as a special case); and a sufficient incompatibility-breaking condition for nonunital channels yielding a sufficient unsteerability criterion for arbitrary two-qubit states.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization on the unital side and constructive sufficient conditions on the nonunital side, unifying incompatibility-breaking and steering results for two-qubit systems.

title: Quantum Magnonics: Quantum States Generation and Applications
comment: 42 pages, 26 figures. Invited Topical Review by Quantum Science and Technology
summary: Hybrid systems based on magnons in ferromagnetic materials, such as yttrium iron garnet, have achieved remarkable development in the last decade. These include the coupling of magnons to microwave and optical photons, superconducting qubits, phonons, spins, the center-of-mass motion of a ferromagnet, etc. Here, we review both the experimental and theoretical progress in this field, focusing on the generation of magnonic quantum states and their applications in a broad range of fields. Since the strong coupling is a prerequisite for achieving coherent quantum control of magnons and preparing magnonic quantum states, we start by introducing representative strong-coupling experiments in cavity magnonics, then review a series of protocols for creating various magnonic quantum states, such as Fock, cat, squeezed, and entangled states, and discuss their potential applications in macroscopic quantum studies, quantum information science, quantum sensing, magnonic quantum devices, dark matter detection, and so on. Finally, we summarize the review and give an outlook for the future study of quantum magnonics.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum magnonics, covering strong-coupling experiments in cavity magnonics, protocols for generating magnonic quantum states (Fock, cat, squeezed, and entangled states), and their applications in macroscopic quantum studies, quantum information, quantum sensing, magnonic quantum devices, and dark matter detection.
AI.motivation: Hybrid systems based on magnons in ferromagnetic materials like yttrium iron garnet have advanced significantly in the past decade, warranting a systematic review of experimental and theoretical progress in generating magnonic quantum states, which are prerequisites for coherent quantum control and broad applications.
AI.method: The paper reviews both experimental and theoretical progress by first introducing representative strong-coupling experiments in cavity magnonics as the foundation for coherent quantum control, then systematically covering protocols for creating magnonic quantum states including Fock, cat, squeezed, and entangled states.
AI.result: The review consolidates achievements in coupling magnons to microwave/optical photons, superconducting qubits, phonons, spins, and center-of-mass motion, while presenting a series of protocols for generating various magnonic quantum states and their potential applications across multiple fields.
AI.conclusion: The review summarizes the current state of quantum magnonics and provides an outlook for future studies in this rapidly developing field.

title: Resource-efficient quantum-selected configuration interaction for molecular properties
summary: The quantum-selected configuration interaction identifies important determinantal basis functions through real-time evolution of a reference wavefunction and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix in the resulting selected subspace. However, implementing the full electronic Hamiltonian on noisy quantum devices leads to rapidly increasing circuit complexity, limiting its scalability. To address this issue, we identify the dominant fermionic excitation operators and perform reference-state fidelity loss analysis to construct a compact Hamiltonian, reducing computational overhead while retaining high precision. Applied to Group IIIA monofluorides (BF, AlF, GaF, InF, and TlF), the proposed framework achieves a near-quadratic improvement in Hamiltonian-term scaling, enabling resource-efficient simulations. We employ this framework to compute the relativistic ground-state energies and permanent electric dipole moments (PDMs) of the systems under consideration. After validating the framework via simulations, we demonstrate hardware execution for AlF and TlF on the IBM Marrakesh processor using active spaces of up to 20 qubits. For a 20-qubit TlF system, the reduced Hamiltonian yields a reduction of higher than $ 98\%$ in both circuit depth and two-qubit gate counts, with the resulting PDMs from quantum hardware matching complete active space configuration interaction values within $99.99\%$. These results demonstrate the scalability of this approach on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework that constructs a compact Hamiltonian for quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) by identifying dominant fermionic excitation operators and analyzing reference-state fidelity loss. Applied to Group IIIA monofluorides, it achieves near-quadratic improvement in Hamiltonian-term scaling. Hardware demonstrations on IBM Marrakesh for AlF and TlF (up to 20 qubits) show >98% reduction in circuit depth and two-qubit gate counts for TlF, with PDMs matching CASCI within 99.99%.
AI.motivation: Full electronic Hamiltonians on noisy quantum devices cause rapidly increasing circuit complexity that limits scalability of QSCI for molecular simulations.
AI.method: Identify dominant fermionic excitation operators and conduct reference-state fidelity loss analysis to construct a reduced (compact) Hamiltonian; apply to relativistic ground-state energy and permanent electric dipole moment (PDM) computations via QSCI for Group IIIA monofluorides (BF, AlF, GaF, InF, TlF).
AI.result: Near-quadratic improvement in Hamiltonian-term scaling; hardware execution on IBM Marrakesh (active spaces up to 20 qubits) for AlF and TlF; for a 20-qubit TlF system, >98% reduction in circuit depth and two-qubit gate counts with PDMs matching CASCI within 99.99%.
AI.conclusion: The reduced-Hamiltonian QSCI framework demonstrates scalability on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices while retaining high accuracy.

title: Quantum machine learning interatomic potential: Application of variational quantum algorithm
summary: This study applied quantum circuit learning, a commonly used hybrid quantum-classical machine learning algorithm, to a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) for predicting the energies of molecules in molecular datasets. We retrained the ANI model using the quantum transfer learning architecture [Mari et al., Quantum, 4:340, 2020] and evaluated numerical accuracy with a quantum circuit simulator. The evaluation confirmed that inserting a quantum circuit into the classical neural network of the MLIP yielded slightly higher accuracy than the fully classical neural network under certain conditions. In particular, the model incorporating a quantum circuit was more effective when the pretraining model had room for improvement in accuracy. These findings may contribute to advancing the application of quantum machine learning for MLIPs.

AI.tldr: This study applies quantum circuit learning (a hybrid quantum-classical machine learning algorithm) to a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) by retraining the ANI model with quantum transfer learning architecture. Using a quantum circuit simulator, the authors found that inserting a quantum circuit into the classical neural network of the MLIP yielded slightly higher accuracy than the fully classical network under certain conditions, particularly when the pretraining model had room for accuracy improvement.
AI.motivation: To advance the application of quantum machine learning to machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), which are crucial for predicting molecular energies but have not yet been widely explored with quantum-enhanced architectures.
AI.method: Applied quantum circuit learning via quantum transfer learning architecture to retrain the ANI model for molecular energy prediction. Numerical accuracy was evaluated using a quantum circuit simulator, comparing hybrid quantum-classical models against a fully classical neural network baseline.
AI.result: The hybrid model with an inserted quantum circuit achieved slightly higher accuracy than the fully classical neural network under certain conditions. The quantum-enhanced model was particularly effective when the pretraining model had room for improvement in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Quantum transfer learning can improve MLIP accuracy under specific conditions, contributing to the advancement of quantum machine learning applications for interatomic potential modeling.

title: Even-harmonic generation through nonequilibrium steady-state symmetry breaking
summary: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in inversion-symmetric systems is typically restricted to odd harmonics by symmetry. Here, we show that this selection rule can be broken without modifying the underlying Hamiltonian. We investigate a boundary-driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain coupled to source and sink reservoirs and demonstrate that dissipative dynamics generates a nonequilibrium steady state carrying a finite DC current. While the SSH Hamiltonian retains inversion symmetry, the current-carrying steady-state density matrix does not, leading to the emergence of even harmonics in the emitted spectrum. Using a correlation-matrix approach based on the Lindblad master equation, we obtain the steady state and calculate the resulting HHG response. We find that the intensity of the even harmonics is directly controlled by the transport current, establishing a link between nonequilibrium charge transport and HHG selection rules. Our results uncover a mechanism for even-harmonic generation that relies solely on nonequilibrium steady-state symmetry breaking and provide a route to probing transport currents through ultrafast nonlinear spectroscopy in centrosymmetric quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that even high-harmonic generation (HHG) can occur in inversion-symmetric systems when the Hamiltonian itself remains centrosymmetric but the nonequilibrium steady state breaks symmetry. Using a boundary-driven SSH chain coupled to reservoirs, they show that a finite DC current in the steady state leads to even harmonics, with even-harmonic intensity directly controlled by the transport current.
AI.motivation: HHG in centrosymmetric systems is conventionally restricted to odd harmonics by symmetry selection rules. The authors ask whether this restriction can be lifted not by modifying the Hamiltonian but by breaking symmetry in the nonequilibrium steady state itself, thereby establishing a new mechanism for even-harmonic generation and linking it to charge transport.
AI.method: The authors investigate a boundary-driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain coupled to source and sink reservoirs. They employ a correlation-matrix approach based on the Lindblad master equation to obtain the nonequilibrium steady state and calculate the resulting HHG spectrum from the current-carrying steady-state density matrix.
AI.result: Dissipative dynamics produces a nonequilibrium steady state carrying a finite DC current. Although the SSH Hamiltonian retains inversion symmetry, the steady-state density matrix does not, resulting in the emergence of even harmonics. The intensity of even harmonics is found to be directly proportional to the transport current, establishing a quantitative link between transport current and HHG selection rules.
AI.conclusion: The work uncovers a novel mechanism for even-harmonic generation based solely on nonequilibrium steady-state symmetry breaking—without altering the underlying Hamiltonian—and proposes a route to probing transport currents via ultrafast nonlinear spectroscopy in centrosymmetric quantum systems.

title: Bayesian Networks of Density Operators
summary: We study quantum analogues of Bayesian networks on a directed acyclic graph (DAG), distinguishing two constructions for positive definite density operators on finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert spaces. The intrinsic construction starts from a joint state and its conditional-independence properties. The extrinsic construction assembles a state sequentially from prescribed local quantum kernels, following an ordering compatible with the arrows of the DAG. For the intrinsic construction, we prove the equivalence of the ordered, local, and global directed Markov properties, together with entropy, recursive-factorization, and logarithmic characterizations. The extrinsic construction always gives a normalized state and recovers each kernel as a conditional on all preceding systems. The same kernel, however, need not be recovered from the marginal on the vertex and its parents; a three-qubit example exhibits this obstruction. We prove that independence of the chosen topological ordering is sufficient exactly for transitive DAGs: every order-invariant kernel family then yields an intrinsically directed Markov state. Finally, we associate a logarithmic candidate with every positive definite state and DAG, prove that it is subnormalized, and show that the trace-one candidate is a directed Markov state. Both the candidate and the excess global information are invariant under DAG Markov equivalence.

AI.tldr: The paper studies two constructions of quantum analogues of Bayesian networks on DAGs: an intrinsic construction based on a joint state's conditional-independence properties, and an extrinsic construction assembling states sequentially from local quantum kernels. It proves equivalence of several directed Markov properties for the intrinsic case, shows order-independence iff the DAG is transitive, and introduces a logarithmic candidate that is invariant under DAG Markov equivalence.
AI.motivation: To extend classical Bayesian network theory to the quantum setting, providing rigorous mathematical foundations for both intrinsic (state-centric) and extrinsic (kernel-centric) constructions of quantum conditional independence on DAGs, and to characterize when these constructions coincide.
AI.method: The paper distinguishes intrinsic vs. extrinsic constructions of quantum states on DAGs. It proves equivalence theorems for ordered, local, and global directed Markov properties using entropy, recursive-factorization, and logarithmic characterizations. It analyzes kernel recovery conditions, constructs a three-qubit counterexample showing failures, proves order-invariance equivalence with transitive DAGs, and defines a logarithmic candidate for general positive definite states.
AI.result: For intrinsic construction, ordered/local/global directed Markov properties are equivalent. Extrinsic construction always normalizes and recovers kernels conditionally, but kernels may not be recovered from vertex-parent marginals (three-qubit counterexample). Order-independence holds exactly for transitive DAGs. A logarithmic candidate is subnormalized, and the trace-one normalized candidate is a directed Markov state; both candidate and excess global information are invariant under DAG Markov equivalence.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete characterization of quantum Bayesian network constructions on DAGs, clarifying when intrinsic and extrinsic approaches agree, and establishing invariance properties under Markov equivalence that mirror classical graphical model theory.

title: Beating the Bad-Cavity Limit via Auxiliary-Emitter Linewidth Squeezing
summary: Strong coupling in cavity QED is conventionally achieved at the expense of either high cavity quality factors or ultrasmall mode volumes, a trade-off that fundamentally constrains practical implementations. Here, we circumvent this limitation by introducing two nonidentical auxiliary emitters with opposite detunings into a bad cavity. This hybrid system supports a subradiant mode that significantly squeeze the effective cavity linewidth, creating an ultra-narrow transmission window at the cavity frequency. As a result, a target emitter placed in this engineered environment exhibits prolonged vacuum Rabi oscillations and resolved spontaneous emission splitting, which are clear signatures of strong coupling, even though the bare cavity remains in the weak-coupling regime. Our scheme thus transforms a bad cavity into an effective platform for strong-coupling physics, with potential applications in quantum computation and quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a scheme to achieve strong coupling in cavity QED without needing high-quality cavities or ultra-small mode volumes, by using two nonidentical auxiliary emitters with opposite detunings in a bad cavity. This creates a subradiant mode that narrows the effective cavity linewidth, enabling strong-coupling signatures like vacuum Rabi oscillations and resolved spontaneous emission splitting for a target emitter, even though the bare cavity is in the weak-coupling regime.
AI.motivation: Conventional strong coupling in cavity QED requires either high cavity quality factors or ultrasmall mode volumes, which fundamentally limits practical implementations. The goal is to circumvent this trade-off and enable strong-coupling physics in a bad cavity.
AI.method: The authors introduce two nonidentical auxiliary emitters with opposite detunings into a bad cavity. This hybrid system supports a subradiant mode that effectively narrows the cavity linewidth, creating an ultra-narrow transmission window at the cavity frequency. A target emitter is then placed in this engineered environment to observe strong-coupling behavior.
AI.result: The engineered system exhibits prolonged vacuum Rabi oscillations and resolved spontaneous emission splitting for the target emitter—clear signatures of strong coupling—despite the bare cavity remaining in the weak-coupling regime. The scheme transforms a bad cavity into an effective platform for strong-coupling physics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme successfully overcomes the conventional quality-factor/mode-volume trade-off, enabling strong coupling in bad cavities with potential applications in quantum computation and quantum sensing.

title: Trainability and Mode Separation of Mixed IQP-QCBMs
summary: Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) based on instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) circuits are promising quantum generative models for their classical trainability. It is known that their ancilla-free form avoids barren plateaus under certain initializations, but remains non-universal. Although adding ancilla qubits raises the expressivity, whether the ancilla-extended model retains local trainability remains unknown. We propose the mixed IQP-QCBM, which generalizes the ancilla-extended circuit as a weighted mixture of ancilla-free IQP circuits, called branches. For a polynomial number of branches, we prove local barren-plateau avoidance from data-agnostic and, under certain assumptions, data-dependent initializations. We further show that the mixed IQP-QCBM can surpass the best ancilla-free IQP circuit only if its branches generate a number of distinct distributions. In particular, we focus on a behavior we call \emph{mode separation}, in which each branch captures a particular feature of the target. Mode separation is hard to attain from an initialization whose branches generate the same distribution: the gradients that would separate them are suppressed while the distributions they generate remain close. This motivates \emph{cluster initialization}, which assigns a different unsupervised data cluster to each branch and provides an initial degree of mode separation. Exact calculations on two 16-bit datasets support the barren-plateau and gradient-suppression claims. On four benchmarks, binary clusters, a two-dimensional Ising model, binarized MNIST, and a 484-spin glass, cluster initialization converges fastest and reaches the lowest mean test $\mathrm{MMD}^2$. We observe that, when achieving the lowest test $\mathrm{MMD}^2$, the mixed IQP-QCBM contains branches specialized to distinguishable data features such as blob patterns, magnetization sectors, or digit shapes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the mixed IQP-QCBM, which generalizes ancilla-extended quantum circuit Born machines as a weighted mixture of ancilla-free IQP circuits (branches). It proves local barren-plateau avoidance for polynomial numbers of branches from data-agnostic and data-dependent initializations, shows that surpassing the best ancilla-free circuit requires branches generating distinct distributions, and introduces cluster initialization that assigns each branch to an unsupervised data cluster to achieve mode separation. Experiments on 16-bit datasets and four benchmarks (binary clusters, 2D Ising model, binarized MNIST, 484-spin glass) show cluster initialization converges fastest and achieves the lowest mean test MMD².
AI.motivation: Ancilla-free IQP-based QCBMs are classically trainable and avoid barren plateaus under certain initializations but are non-universal. Adding ancilla qubits increases expressivity, but whether the ancilla-extended model retains local trainability is unknown. The paper aims to bridge this gap by proposing a model that combines the trainability of ancilla-free circuits with enhanced expressivity.
AI.method: The paper proposes the mixed IQP-QCBM, a weighted mixture of ancilla-free IQP circuits (branches). It proves local barren-plateau avoidance for polynomial numbers of branches from data-agnostic and, under certain assumptions, data-dependent initializations. It analyzes mode separation—a behavior where each branch captures a particular feature of the target—and shows it is hard to attain from initialization where branches generate the same distribution due to suppressed gradients. It introduces cluster initialization, which assigns a different unsupervised data cluster to each branch to provide an initial degree of mode separation.
AI.result: Exact calculations on two 16-bit datasets support the barren-plateau and gradient-suppression claims. On four benchmarks (binary clusters, 2D Ising model, binarized MNIST, and a 484-spin glass), cluster initialization converges fastest and reaches the lowest mean test MMD². When achieving the lowest test MMD², the mixed IQP-QCBM contains branches specialized to distinguishable data features such as blob patterns, magnetization sectors, or digit shapes.
AI.conclusion: The mixed IQP-QCBM generalizes ancilla-extended circuits while preserving trainability, and cluster initialization enables mode separation, allowing each branch to specialize on distinct data features. This leads to faster convergence and better generative performance across benchmarks compared to other initialization strategies.

title: Witness robustness: An operational quantifier of measurement resources via free state discrimination
summary: We introduce the witness robustness of quantum measurements, a resource quantifier whose admissible noise consists of tuples of free-state witnesses rather than physical measurements. We establish its operational interpretation: it quantifies the maximal advantage that a measurement can provide over free measurements in discriminating an ensemble composed entirely of free states. Unlike the standard and generalized robustnesses, the witness robustness is not faithful in general, reflecting the fact that a resourceful measurement need not be useful when only free states can be prepared. We identify conditions under which faithfulness is recovered and show that, in resource theories admitting a resource-destroying map, the witness robustness vanishes for every measurement. We also establish fundamental properties, including convexity and monotonicity. Finally, we derive analytical results for projective measurements in single-qubit magic and for binary pure-state projective measurements in the two-qubit PPT entanglement theory.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "witness robustness" as a new resource quantifier for quantum measurements, where admissible noise consists of tuples of free-state witnesses rather than physical measurements. It establishes the operational interpretation, faithfulness conditions, fundamental properties (convexity, monotonicity), and analytical results for specific resource theories (single-qubit magic and two-qubit PPT entanglement).
AI.motivation: Standard and generalized robustness measures for quantum measurements assume admissible noise must be physical measurements, which can be restrictive. The authors propose a witness robustness that relaxes this constraint by allowing tuples of free-state witnesses as noise, aiming to provide a new quantifier with a clear operational interpretation tied to ensemble discrimination.
AI.method: The authors define the witness robustness as a resource quantifier whose noise model consists of tuples of free-state witnesses. They establish its operational interpretation via ensemble discrimination of free states, analyze faithfulness conditions, study its behavior under resource-destroying maps, prove fundamental properties such as convexity and monotonicity, and derive analytical results for projective measurements in single-qubit magic (Wigner negativity) and binary pure-state projective measurements in two-qubit PPT entanglement theory.
AI.result: The witness robustness is shown to quantify the maximal advantage a measurement can provide over free measurements in discriminating an ensemble of free states. Unlike standard and generalized robustnesses, it is not faithful in general, reflecting that resourceful measurements need not be useful when only free states are prepared. Faithfulness is recovered under identified conditions. In resource theories admitting a resource-destroying map, the witness robustness vanishes for every measurement. Convexity and monotonicity are established. Analytical results are derived for single-qubit magic and two-qubit PPT entanglement cases.
AI.conclusion: The witness robustness offers a distinct and operationally meaningful resource quantifier for quantum measurements, with behavior (e.g., non-faithfulness) that reflects the practical utility of a measurement relative to free-state preparation. Its analytical tractability in specific theories makes it a valuable tool for studying measurement resources.

title: Interconnection of Quantum Networks at Urban scale: Analysis of Temporal Stability of Entangled Photon Sources
comment: Accepted manuscript for publication in IEEE QCE26. This work has been funded by the European Union under Horizon Europe ERC-CoG grant QNattyNet ("Quantum-Native Communication Networks: from Quantum Message to Quantum Functioning"), n.101169850. Details at https://qnattynet.quantuminternet.it
summary: Time synchronization is a fundamental requirement in entanglement-based quantum networks, where the indistinguishability of photons in the time domain is essential for enabling Hong-Ou-Mandel interference and entanglement swapping. In addition to precise temporal alignment, it is equally crucial to ensure the stability of the reference clock over time, as even small fluctuations can degrade the overall performance of the network. In this work, we investigate the stability of clock synchronization for entanglement distribution based on entangled-photon sources operating in the telecommunication C-band. Temporal correlations between photon detection events are analyzed using time-tagged coincidence measurements, enabling the extraction of synchronization peaks and their long-term stability. Experimental results demonstrate that, once locked, the sources exhibit stable temporal correlations over an 8-hour acquisition period, with a maximum observed drift of approximately 120 ps, primarily associated with long fiber links. The width of the correlation peak remains consistent with detector jitter, indicating negligible additional system-induced temporal broadening. A central result of this work is the experimental synchronization between two entanglement-photon sources in a realistic metropolitan deployment, where entanglement distribution is performed over existing telecommunication infrastructure characterized by non-negligible losses and background noise. In this scenario, despite the presence of significant imperfections introduced by the metropolitan-scale fiber network, the observed correlations remain clearly detectable and are consistently well-approximated by Gaussian statistics. This confirms that the two sources can be reliably synchronized not only in controlled laboratory conditions but also under real-world operating constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the stability of clock synchronization for entanglement distribution using entangled-photon sources in the C-band, demonstrating stable temporal correlations over an 8-hour period with a maximum drift of ~120 ps (attributed to long fiber links), and successfully synchronizing two entangled-photon sources in a realistic metropolitan fiber network with non-negligible losses and noise, where correlations remain clearly detectable and well-approximated by Gaussian statistics.
AI.motivation: Time synchronization is a fundamental requirement in entanglement-based quantum networks, requiring both precise temporal alignment and long-term reference clock stability, as small fluctuations can degrade overall network performance.
AI.method: The authors use time-tagged coincidence measurements to analyze temporal correlations between photon detection events from entangled-photon sources, extracting synchronization peaks and evaluating their long-term stability. Experiments are conducted in both controlled laboratory conditions and a realistic metropolitan deployment over existing telecommunications infrastructure.
AI.result: Once locked, the sources exhibit stable temporal correlations over an 8-hour acquisition period with a maximum observed drift of ~120 ps, primarily associated with long fiber links. The correlation peak width remains consistent with detector jitter, indicating negligible additional system-induced temporal broadening. In the metropolitan deployment, correlations remain clearly detectable despite losses and background noise, and are consistently well-approximated by Gaussian statistics.
AI.conclusion: Two entangled-photon sources can be reliably synchronized not only under controlled laboratory conditions but also under real-world metropolitan operating constraints, confirming the feasibility of stable clock synchronization for entanglement-based quantum networks in practical deployments.

title: Iterative quantum algorithms for the minimum vertex cover problem based on continuous-time quantum walks
summary: We introduce a constraint-preserving hybrid quantum-classical greedy framework for the minimum vertex cover problem, which extends directly to maximum independent set by bitwise complementation. The framework uses projected Pauli-X terms whose sum preserves the feasible subspace and acts within it exactly as the adjacency matrix of a layered graph of feasible covers. This graph is connected, so every feasible cover is linked to the configuration containing all vertices by a sequence of allowed single-vertex flips. Starting from this configuration, the corresponding continuous-time quantum walk propagates amplitude into layers containing progressively smaller covers. We rank vertices using either their marginal cover probabilities or the expected cover size obtained after fixing each candidate vertex in the cover, and use these rankings to guide recursive greedy reductions. Across several random-graph families, with walk times fixed using independent calibration ensembles, the quantum-informed algorithms achieve lower mean approximation ratios and solve a larger fraction of instances optimally than their corresponding classical greedy baselines. The conditioned-energy strategy performs best on the tested instances and retains algorithmic performance close to the exact continuous-time limit under low-depth Trotterisation. For bounded-degree graphs, each Trotter layer has circuit depth independent of system size, and the framework requires neither penalty terms nor variational training.

AI.tldr: A constraint-preserving hybrid quantum-classical greedy framework for minimum vertex cover / maximum independent set, using projected Pauli-X terms and continuous-time quantum walks to guide recursive greedy reductions, outperforming classical greedy baselines on random graphs.
AI.motivation: Minimum vertex cover and maximum independent set are NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems with broad applications. Greedy algorithms provide efficient but suboptimal heuristics, and quantum approaches typically require penalty terms or variational training that complicate or degrade performance. The authors seek a quantum-informed greedy strategy that preserves the feasible subspace, avoids penalties, and improves on classical baselines.
AI.method: The framework projects Pauli-X terms so their sum preserves the feasible subspace and acts within it exactly as the adjacency matrix of a layered graph of feasible covers. This graph is connected, enabling a continuous-time quantum walk from the all-vertices configuration to propagate amplitude into layers of progressively smaller covers. Vertex rankings are derived from either marginal cover probabilities or expected cover sizes after fixing each candidate, guiding recursive greedy reductions. Walk times are fixed using independent calibration ensembles, and low-depth Trotterisation (with constant circuit depth for bounded-degree graphs) is used without penalty terms or variational training.
AI.result: Across several random-graph families, the quantum-informed algorithms achieve lower mean approximation ratios and solve a larger fraction of instances optimally than their classical greedy baselines. The conditioned-energy strategy performs best, retaining performance close to the exact continuous-time limit under low-depth Trotterisation.
AI.conclusion: The constraint-preserving quantum-classical greedy framework is a practical, penalty-free, and training-free approach that consistently outperforms classical greedy heuristics for minimum vertex cover and maximum independent set, with quantum hardware feasibility supported by system-size-independent circuit depth on bounded-degree graphs.

title: Design of a Quantum Error Correction Decoder Exploiting Temporal Parallelism
comment: 11 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE) 2026
summary: In the pursuit of fault-tolerant quantum computing, low-latency quantum error correction (QEC) is essential to prevent rapid error accumulation within the syndrome measurement cycle. In this work, we propose a microarchitecture that implements the sandwich decoding method using the Union-Find algorithm by exploiting temporal parallelism, and we present an ASIC implementation. Through logic synthesis and simulation, we show that the proposed decoder achieves an average latency reduction of 35% at code distance d = 21 compared with a conventional batch Union-Find decoder, while maintaining a comparable logical error threshold of approximately 1.5% under phenomenological noise.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a microarchitecture implementing the sandwich decoding method using the Union-Find algorithm with temporal parallelism, validated through an ASIC implementation and logic synthesis. It achieves a 35% average latency reduction at code distance d=21 compared to a conventional batch Union-Find decoder while maintaining a comparable logical error threshold of ~1.5% under phenomenological noise.
AI.motivation: Low-latency quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing to prevent rapid error accumulation within the syndrome measurement cycle.
AI.method: The authors propose a microarchitecture that implements the sandwich decoding method using the Union-Find algorithm by exploiting temporal parallelism, and present an ASIC implementation evaluated through logic synthesis and simulation.
AI.result: The proposed decoder achieves an average latency reduction of 35% at code distance d=21 compared with a conventional batch Union-Find decoder, while maintaining a comparable logical error threshold of approximately 1.5% under phenomenological noise.
AI.conclusion: Temporal parallelism in sandwich decoding with Union-Find can significantly reduce decoding latency without compromising logical error threshold, making it a viable approach for low-latency QEC in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Complementary Matrix-Gated QKAN Fast-Weight Programmers for Quantum Dynamics Forecasting
summary: Sequence models must decide what to write into memory and what to retain. In quantum and quantum-inspired sequence learning, nonlinear recurrent updates often require repeated circuit evaluations and sequential backpropagation through time, making long contexts costly. Gated fast-weight programmers (FWPs) based on quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (QKANs) alleviate this bottleneck by storing context in time-varying fast parameters. However, their scalar gate applies one retention-write balance to every fast-state coordinate, forcing all parameters to share a memory timescale. We introduce Self-Modulating QKAN-based FWPs, which replace this broadcast gate with low-rank-generated element-wise modulation of the new-proposal branch, a bounded old-state branch, or both. We further propose Complementary Matrix Gating (CMG), which uses one sigmoid matrix gate to retain the old state and its complement to write the new proposal. CMG provides coordinate-wise memory control while preserving the bounded convex update and affine prefix-scan structure of scalar gating, at the modulation-head cost of a single-branch rule. We compare four self-modulating rules with scalar gating across four FWP architectures combining classical and QKAN-based slow and fast programmers. Across seven single-step forecasting benchmarks and five sequence lengths, CMG gives the most consistent improvements for architectures whose fast programmer incorporates a QKAN-based module. In direct multi-step forecasting of Jaynes-Cummings and transmon-resonator dynamics simulated with CUDA-Q Dynamics, CMG models maintain mean-squared errors on the order of 0.001 or lower across forecasting horizons of 4, 8, and 16 steps, while improving on their scalar-gated counterparts by at least 91.2%. These results establish coordinate-wise complementary modulation as a stable and effective update for QKAN-based FWPs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Self-Modulating QKAN-based fast-weight programmers (FWPs) that replace scalar gate-based memory control with low-rank-generated element-wise modulation of fast-state coordinates. A novel Complementary Matrix Gating (CMG) mechanism uses a sigmoid matrix gate to retain old state and its complement to write new proposals, enabling coordinate-wise memory control while preserving bounded convex update and affine prefix-scan structure. CMG shows consistent improvements over scalar gating across seven single-step forecasting benchmarks and five sequence lengths, and achieves MSE ≤ 0.001 with ≥91.2% improvement over scalar-gated counterparts in multi-step forecasting of quantum dynamics.
AI.motivation: Scalar gating in existing QKAN-based FWPs applies a single retention-write balance to all fast-state coordinates, forcing all parameters to share a uniform memory timescale. This limits the model's ability to selectively retain or write information at different coordinate levels, motivating the need for coordinate-wise memory control in quantum-inspired sequence learning.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) Self-Modulating QKAN-based FWPs that use low-rank-generated element-wise modulation applied to the new-proposal branch, a bounded old-state branch, or both; and (2) Complementary Matrix Gating (CMG), which uses one sigmoid matrix gate to retain the old state and its complement to write the new proposal. CMG maintains the bounded convex update and affine prefix-scan structure of scalar gating while enabling coordinate-wise memory control at the cost of a single-branch modulation head.
AI.result: Across four FWP architectures combining classical and QKAN-based slow/fast programmers, seven single-step forecasting benchmarks, and five sequence lengths, CMG provides the most consistent improvements for architectures with QKAN-based fast programmer modules. In multi-step forecasting of Jaynes-Cummings and transmon-resonator dynamics (CUDA-Q Dynamics), CMG models maintain MSE ≤ 0.001 across horizons of 4, 8, and 16 steps, improving on scalar-gated counterparts by at least 91.2%.
AI.conclusion: Coordinate-wise complementary modulation is established as a stable and effective update rule for QKAN-based FWPs, addressing the memory timescale sharing limitation of scalar gating and demonstrating significant performance gains in both single-step and multi-step forecasting tasks.

title: A CPU+DCU Heterogeneous Parallel Framework for Post-Processing Reconstruction in Quantum Circuit Cutting
summary: In the NISQ era, limited qubit resources make it difficult to execute large quantum circuits directly on real hardware. Quantum circuit cutting mitigates this limitation by decomposing a large circuit into smaller subcircuits, but it shifts substantial overhead to classical post-processing. As circuit size, complexity, and cut count increase, reconstruction becomes a major computational and storage bottleneck. This paper presents a CPU+DCU heterogeneous parallel framework for circuit-cutting post-processing reconstruction. Instead of constructing a dense $2^n$-dimensional probability vector or returning only high-probability states, the framework reconstructs the nonzero-probability states in the original output distribution from subcircuit measurement results. It combines heterogeneous CPU+DCU execution with a high/low-word integer representation for global basis-state indices beyond 64 bits and a three-level cooperative storage mechanism spanning device memory, host memory, and out-of-core storage. Experiments on the Songshan supercomputer show that the framework maintains high reconstruction fidelity while achieving up to $259\times$ speedup over an optimized serial baseline on linear-cluster states and up to $4\times$ speedup over a homogeneous CPU-parallel method on random circuits. The framework can also complete reconstruction tasks at the hundred-qubit scale. These results demonstrate that HPC-oriented heterogeneous reconstruction can effectively alleviate the classical post-processing bottleneck and improve reconstruction scalability.

It achieves up to 259× speedup over serial baselines and up to 4× speedup over homogeneous CPU-parallel methods, capable of handling hundred-qubit scale reconstruction tasks on the Songshan supercomputer.

As circuit size, complexity, and cut count increase, reconstruction becomes a major computational and storage bottleneck that needs to be addressed.

title: Exponential Advantage of Multipartite Entanglement over Quantum Communication with Applications to Bounded-Storage Cryptography
comment: 5.25 pages (double-column) + 3.5 pages (single-column); 2 figures; Comments are welcome
summary: We establish an exponential communication advantage enabled by multipartite quantum entanglement. Building on the bipartite Hidden Matching problem, we introduce a communication task involving multiple spatially separated senders and a single receiver. We show that a shared Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state enables completion of this task using only logarithmically many bits of classical communication from each sender. In contrast, without preshared entanglement, any protocol achieving high success probability requires polynomial communication from at least one sender, even when \emph{quantum} communication is allowed. Thus, classical communication assisted by multipartite entanglement can be exponentially more powerful than quantum communication without preshared entanglement. As a cryptographic application, we construct a seeded two-source randomness extractor and establish an exponential separation between entangled and unentangled quantum side-information. Specifically, compromising the extractor with two unentangled quantum states storing information about the two sources, respectively, requires polynomial-size memory, whereas exponentially smaller quantum memory suffices in the presence of a small amount of shared entanglement.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes an exponential communication complexity advantage enabled by multipartite quantum entanglement. Using a multipartite extension of the Hidden Matching problem with multiple senders and one receiver, the authors show that shared GHZ states allow completion with logarithmic classical communication per sender, while any protocol without preshared entanglement requires polynomial communication even if quantum communication is permitted. A cryptographic application yields a seeded two-source randomness extractor with an exponential separation between entangled and unentangled quantum side-information.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate an exponential quantum advantage in communication complexity that specifically relies on multipartite entanglement (beyond bipartite settings), and to explore its cryptographic implications for randomness extraction in the presence of quantum side-information.
AI.method: The authors generalize the bipartite Hidden Matching problem to a multipartite communication task involving multiple spatially separated senders and a single receiver. They analyze the protocol's performance with shared GHZ entanglement using logarithmic classical communication, and prove lower bounds showing polynomial communication is required without preshared entanglement, even allowing quantum communication. They then construct a seeded two-source randomness extractor based on this separation and analyze its security against entangled vs. unentangled quantum side-information.
AI.result: An exponential separation is established: with shared GHZ entanglement, only logarithmically many bits of classical communication per sender are needed, whereas polynomial communication is required from at least one sender without preshared entanglement—even when quantum communication is allowed. For the extractor application, exponential separation is shown: polynomial-size memory is needed for unentangled quantum side-information, while exponentially smaller quantum memory suffices with small shared entanglement.
AI.conclusion: Multipartite entanglement enables an exponential communication advantage over quantum communication without preshared entanglement. This separation has direct cryptographic consequences, yielding a seeded two-source randomness extractor that exhibits an exponential gap in the required quantum memory between entangled and unentangled side-information settings.

title: Towards Quantum Networks: Characterizing Raman Noise over Metropolitan-scale Fiber Network
comment: Invited Paper in IEEE SMARTCOMP. This work has been funded by the European Union under Horizon Europe ERC-CoG grant QNattyNet ("Quantum-Native Communication Networks: from Quantum Message to Quantum Functioning"), n.101169850. Details at https://qnattynet.quantuminternet.it
summary: The coexistence of quantum and classical signals in optical fiber infrastructures represents a major challenge for large-scale quantum networks, as noise sources such as Raman scattering can significantly impact entanglement distribution, and the quantum protocols based on it. In this work, we analyze Raman scattering in the C-band, used for entanglement distribution, generated by a classical the O-band signal. The main contribution of this study lays in investigating these effects in a real metropolitan-fiber network, moving beyond controlled laboratory experiments to deployed telecommunication environments. Measurements are performed over a 7 km metropolitan fiber link using commercial sources and narrowband lasers. The experimental results shows good agreement between the measurements taken under laboratory conditions, although, within the metropolitan-scale loop, localized spectral anomalies are observed in the deployed fibers. Therefore, our results show that, whenever a quantum signal propagates in the C-band alongside an O-band classical channel within the same fiber, careful selection of the operating frequency is required, as Raman scattering and other real-world noise sources can significantly affect the quality and stability of the quantum transmission. In particular, we identify spectral regions that are less affected by Raman noise, thereby providing practical guidelines for optimal quantum channel allocation. We demonstrate that Raman-induced noise constitutes a dominant contribution to the quantum signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in realistic deployments, beyond background and detector noise. Overall, our findings offer practical insights for deploying quantum communication systems over existing fiber networks, supporting the development of robust and scalable quantum infrastructures.

It identifies spectral regions less affected by Raman noise and shows that Raman-induced noise dominates the quantum SNR in realistic deployments, providing practical guidelines for optimal quantum channel allocation.
AI.motivation: The coexistence of quantum and classical signals in optical fiber infrastructures is a major challenge for large-scale quantum networks, as noise sources like Raman scattering can significantly impact entanglement distribution and related quantum protocols. Most previous studies were confined to controlled laboratory experiments, leaving a gap in understanding these effects in real deployed telecommunication environments.
AI.method: Measurements were performed over a 7 km metropolitan fiber link using commercial sources and narrowband lasers. The study analyzes Raman scattering in the C-band generated by a classical O-band signal, comparing laboratory conditions with real-world metropolitan deployments.
AI.result: Experimental results show good agreement between laboratory and field measurements, though localized spectral anomalies were observed in the deployed metropolitan-scale fibers. Raman-induced noise was identified as a dominant contribution to the quantum signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), exceeding background and detector noise. Spectral regions less affected by Raman noise were identified.
AI.conclusion: When a quantum signal propagates in the C-band alongside an O-band classical channel in the same fiber, careful selection of the operating frequency is required. The findings provide practical guidelines for optimal quantum channel allocation and practical insights for deploying quantum communication systems over existing fiber networks, supporting robust and scalable quantum infrastructures.

title: Bridging continuous control and Floquet driving for charging many-body spin chains
comment: Main text: 20 pages, 5 figures. Submitted as Chapter 3 in Springer series: Advances in Atoms and Single Molecule Machines Vol. 17: "Single Atom (Molecule) Energy Storage: Towards a Quantum Battery". Editor: Christian Joachim
summary: Recent advances in quantum information and quantum thermodynamics have reshaped the understanding of energy storage at the microscopic scale, paving the way toward protocols for storing and transferring energy in quantum devices. These systems, known as quantum batteries, offer a conceptual alternative to conventional macroscopic chemical batteries by exploiting quantum coherence, correlations, and many-body dynamics. By navigating the landscape of established spin-based quantum batteries, we review existing charging and work-extraction protocols, as well as the impact of external factors on their performance. Motivated by Floquet-engineered proposals, we further establish a connection between continuously and periodically driven spin chains as platforms for quantum energy storage. Finally, we survey experimental realizations and proposals, highlighting their implementability and scalability in current and near-term quantum technologies.
